title: Designing an LLC Converter
subject: Power Electronics
blurb: A spec sheet in, a tank and a bill of materials out. The procedure, the constraints that fight it, and one worked example end to end.
prerequisites: FHA gain curve and the m/Q parameters

slides.title:
Designing an
LLC Converter
slides.lead: Volt 01 explained the topology. This one turns a specification into Lr, Cr, Lm, a turns ratio, and part numbers you can actually order.

slides.title:
Four numbers are handed to you,
and three are yours to pick
slides.lead: Every LLC design begins the same way. Knowing which quantities are constraints and which are degrees of freedom is most of the discipline — the common failure is treating Q as a knob.

columns.label: Given by the specification
items: V<sub>in</sub> nominal, and the low-line corner you must hold
V<sub>out</sub> and the regulation window
P<sub>out</sub> at full load, and the light-load floor
Efficiency target and the enclosure that sets your thermal budget

columns.label: Yours to choose
items: fr — trades magnetics size against core and gate loss
m — trades gain range against circulating current
tdead — trades ZVS margin against conduction window
The FET, which sets C<sub>o(tr)</sub> and therefore constrains L<sub>m</sub>

slides.callout: Q is on neither list. Q is what your chosen Lr/Cr ratio becomes at the load the specification hands you. You choose the ratio; the load chooses Q.

slides.title:
Fix the turns ratio so nominal
input parks you on fr
slides.lead: At fr the gain is 1 regardless of load, the tank is purely resistive, and the converter is at its most efficient. Design so the input you see most of the time puts you there.

formulas.label: Turns ratio
formulas.note: The half comes from the half-bridge: the tank sees half the bus. Vf is the rectifier drop — small with synchronous rectification, not negligible with Schottkys at low Vout.

formulas.label: Gain you must produce
formulas.note: Evaluate at the low-line corner. That number is the entire reason the tank needs any boost capability at all.

points.text: Larger n lowers primary current for the same power, which helps conduction loss on the side where the voltage is high.
But larger n raises the gain demanded at low line, which forces smaller m and more circulating current.
The PFC stage sets your job. A well-regulated 390 V bus that only sags during hold-up needs far less boost than a wide-input design.

slides.callout: Hold-up time is where this bites. If the bus is allowed to droop to 330 V while the output stays in regulation, you have just specified M = 1.18 and the whole tank follows from it.

slides.title:
Q has a ceiling,
and it is not yours
slides.lead: Load Q too heavily and the gain curve flattens below what low line demands, or worse, the operating point crosses into the capacitive region. There is a maximum Q the design tolerates, and it must be computed at the worst corner.

formulas.label: Q as it is actually set
formulas.note: R<sub>ac</sub> = 8n²V<sub>out</sub>²/π²P<sub>out</sub>. Heavy load means small R<sub>ac</sub> means large Q. You pick the impedance ratio; the specification picks the rest.

formulas.label: The ceiling
formulas.expression: QZVS : where the input impedance phase reaches zero
formulas.note: Evaluate at maximum output power and minimum input voltage — the corner where the phase margin is smallest. Then back off.

points.text: Take 5 to 10% margin below QZVS. Component tolerance, temperature drift on Cr, and transient overshoot all eat into it.
Overload walks you off the edge. Exceed the load the Qmax curve was drawn for and the operating point crosses into capacitive operation, where hard switching can destroy the primary FETs.
This is why the current limit is a tank parameter, not just a controller setting. The two are specified together or not at all.

slides.callout: Design at full load, low line. Every other operating point is easier, and a design that survives that corner survives the rest by construction.

slides.title:
Pick m so the peak clears
your required gain

points.text: The peak gain has no closed form. You cannot solve the FHA equation for it — it is found numerically, or read from published peak-gain-versus-Q curves plotted for each m.
Lower m raises the peak and widens the boost region, at the cost of circulating current and full-load efficiency.
Leave 10 to 20% margin above the required gain, for start-up and load transients. FHA overestimates the real peak, so the margin is not optional.
Most designs land at m between 3 and 8. Below 3 the efficiency penalty is severe; above 8 there is barely any boost left.

slides.callout: Drag m down and watch the peak rise past the required-gain line. Then look at what happens to Lm — you have just bought gain range with circulating current.

slides.title:
Now the tank falls out
in three lines
slides.lead: With fr, m and Q settled, there is nothing left to decide. The resonant components are determined, and the only remaining question is whether the resulting Lm survives the ZVS check on the next slide.

formulas.label: The series pair
formulas.note: Two equations, two unknowns: Q fixes the ratio √(Lr/Cr), fr fixes the product LrCr. Together they pin both values exactly.

formulas.label: The magnetising inductance
formulas.note: A provisional value only. It is the gain curve's opinion of Lm, and the dead time may well overrule it.

points.text: Round to real parts, then recompute. Cr comes in E12 values and fr moves when you round it. Recalculate fr from the parts you can actually buy, not the other way round.
Lr is often the transformer leakage. If you are integrating it, this number is a winding-construction target, not a component you order.

slides.callout: Everything to this point came from the gain curve alone. The gain curve does not know about your FETs, and that is the subject of the next slide.

slides.title:
Check Lm against
the dead time
slides.widgetTitle: Interactive LLC tank designer — ZVS check

points.text: Lm ≤ tdead / (16·Co(tr)·fr). If the provisional Lm exceeds this, ZVS does not happen and no amount of gain-curve tuning fixes it.
Three ways out. Lengthen tdead, choose a FET with less output charge, or reduce m — in that order of preference, because the third one costs efficiency everywhere.
Co(tr), not datasheet Coss. Use the charge-equivalent value across the full Vds swing. The spot capacitance at rated voltage will flatter the design by a wide margin.
Longer dead time is not free. It eats conduction window and narrows the achievable gain at the frequency extremes.

slides.callout: Nudge Co(tr) up by a few tens of picofarads and the ceiling drops below the Lm you wanted. The default design is only 6% clear of it — that is how narrow this constraint really is, and why FET selection belongs in the tank design rather than after it.

slides.title:
The numbers you actually
order parts from

points.text: ILr rms sizes the primary FET conduction loss, the resonant inductor wire, and the primary winding. It combines the reflected load current with the magnetising current.
VCr peak is the DC blocking level plus the AC swing across Cr. It routinely lands two to three times the rail — this is why Cr is a 630 V part in a 390 V converter.
Isec rms sizes the rectifier and the secondary winding, where the current is large and the copper is short and fat.
These are FHA estimates at fr. Good enough to select parts and set a thermal budget. Not good enough to skip the simulation.

slides.callout: A design is not finished when L<sub>r</sub>, C<sub>r</sub> and L<sub>m</sub> exist. It is finished when every part in the loop has a rating with margin against these numbers at the worst corner.

slides.title:
Cr is a resonant component,
not a decoupling cap
slides.lead: It carries the full resonant current continuously, sets fr directly, and sees a peak voltage far above the rail. Substituting the wrong dielectric here changes the converter's resonant frequency in the field, as a function of temperature and bias.

columns.label: What it must survive
items: Peak voltage of roughly V<sub>in</sub>/2 plus the AC swing
Continuous rms current equal to the tank current
Self-heating from ESR at the switching frequency
Whatever the overload transient does before the clamp acts

columns.label: What to specify
items: Film, not class 2 ceramic. X7R loses a large fraction of its capacitance under DC bias
Tolerance tight enough that f<sub>r</sub> stays inside your control range
Ripple current rating checked at f<sub>r</sub>, not at 120 Hz
Consider splitting into two caps to halve the rms current per part

slides.callout: A capacitance error goes into fr as its square root, so a 10% capacitance shift moves the resonant frequency about 5%. Tolerable. A 40% bias-induced loss is not.

slides.title:
The transformer is where
your design actually lives
slides.lead: In most LLC builds Lr is the transformer leakage and Lm is its magnetising inductance, which means two of your three tank values are set by winding geometry and a gap, not by a purchase order.

columns.label: Integrated magnetics
items: One component instead of two, smaller and cheaper
Leakage becomes a designed quantity via winding separation
L<sub>m</sub> set by the gap, tunable during prototyping
Standard approach in high-volume production

columns.label: What it costs you
items: Leakage tolerance is wide and varies with construction
Any winding change is a resonant frequency change
Interleaving reduces AC resistance but also reduces the L<sub>r</sub> you need
A discrete L<sub>r</sub> is bigger and dearer, but it is a number you can trust

slides.callout: Prototype with a discrete inductor so the tank is known, then integrate once the design is proven. Debugging a resonant frequency you cannot measure independently is a bad way to spend a week.

slides.title:
390 V bus,
48 V at 300 W
slides.lead: A telecom-style rectifier stage. The PFC holds 390 V nominal and is allowed to droop to 330 V during hold-up, with the output staying in regulation throughout. Everything below follows from those numbers.

formulas.label: Turns ratio
formulas.note: Gain is 1 at the nominal bus, so the converter sits at fr whenever the line is healthy. Rectifier drop ignored here; with synchronous rectification that is defensible.

formulas.label: Gain at the hold-up corner
formulas.note: An 18% boost requirement. Modest, which is what a well-regulated bus buys you — a universal-input design would be asking for far more.

points.text: Choose fr = 100 kHz. Comfortable for silicon superjunction FETs and ferrite, and it keeps the magnetics at a size that fits the enclosure.
Choose m = 6, Q = 0.4. Peak gain works out at 1.39 against the 1.18 required — a 17% margin, right in the recommended band.
Rac = 8n²Vout²/π²Pout = 103 Ω. This is the load as the tank sees it, and it is what turns the chosen Q into real component values.

slides.callout: Note the order. Nothing was solved for until fr, m and Q were chosen, and each of those was a judgement call bounded by a constraint — not a calculation.

slides.title:
The tank, and the parts
it demands
slides.widgetTitle: Interactive LLC tank designer — worked example

points.text: Lr = 65 µH, Cr = 39 nF, Lm = 327 µH. Round Cr to 39 nF exactly, then recompute fr from the parts you can buy.
ILr = 1.9 A rms at full load, of which roughly 0.9 A is magnetising current that never reaches the output. That is the ZVS fee made numeric.
VCr peak ≈ 306 V. Specify a 630 V film capacitor. The 390 V rail is not the rating that matters.
ZVS check. Evaluated at start-up, the hardest corner, 200 ns and 120 pF give a ceiling near 347 µH against the 327 µH Lm — a pass with only 6% headroom. Comfortable at fr, marginal where it matters.

slides.callout: The widget is loaded with exactly this example. Change one slider at a time and watch which of the four results moves — that coupling is the design.

slides.title:
What the spreadsheet
has not checked
slides.lead: FHA sized the tank at one operating point. The corners it never looked at are where prototypes fail, and every item below has to be verified in simulation before a board is fabricated.

columns.label: Simulate these corners
items: Start-up. Output at zero demands enormous gain; sweep the frequency down from well above fr
No load. The light-load curve peaks hard and frequency control runs out of range; burst mode is the usual answer
Output short. The loop chases gain downward into the capacitive region
Hold-up droop with a step load applied at the same moment

columns.label: Then check the hardware
items: Minimum frequency clamp present and set below fmin but above the peak locus
Measured Lr and Lm on the built transformer, not the design values
Cr capacitance at operating bias and temperature, not at 1 kHz on the bench
Vds at turn-on observed at light load and high line, the hardest ZVS corner

slides.callout: The most common production failure is not a mistuned tank. It is a controller with no low-frequency clamp meeting a transient nobody simulated.

slides.title: The procedure, in order
slides.lead: Six steps, two of which are judgement calls and four of which are arithmetic. Knowing which is which is the difference between designing an LLC and copying one.

formulas.label: The two judgement calls
formulas.note: fr trades magnetics size against switching loss. m trades gain range against circulating current. Everything else is bounded by them.

formulas.label: The binding check
formulas.note: The gain curve proposes an Lm. The dead time disposes of it. When they disagree, the dead time wins.

points.text: n from the nominal bus, M from the worst corner. Design at full load and low line; every other point is easier.
Q is a constraint, not a knob. You choose √(Lr/Cr); the load chooses Q.
Finish with stresses. A tank without ratings is not a design.
